read: full: abstract, sections 1-5 (pp. 1-19: introduction and research questions, state of the art, the five research-question analyses with Tables 1-5, discussion, conclusion); skimmed the references (pp. 19-23)
venue_now: arXiv preprint, arXiv:2505.13484v1 of 12 May 2025 (p1 footer; the title page is dated May 21, 2025). The text shows no venue, consistent with the May entry.
what_it_is: Heesch et al. evaluate four LLMs on engineering tasks drawn from production settings, around five research questions: world models, transitional and non-local relations, implicit design intentions, temporal and causal reasoning, and forecasting (pp. 2-3). Over 80 new questions come from a real glass-foaming plant and a simulated discrete-manufacturing plant (45 on world models, 20 on relations, the rest on causal and diagnostic modelling), 20 more ask the models to infer design intent from product function structures, and forecasting is tested on 200 time-series samples from two cyber-physical-system datasets (pp. 3, 6-8, 10, 14). Each question is posed several times, only the least accurate answer is scored, on a three-point scale (0 incorrect; 0.5 partially correct, junior-engineer level; 1 comprehensive, senior-engineer level), and scores are averaged per category; forecasting is scored by MSE against LSTM and DLinear baselines (pp. 5, 7, 15). The models handle local, sequential reasoning but struggle with type-level abstraction, multi-variable dependencies, formal and physical modelling, and forecasting (pp. 1, 9-17).
domain: engineering: production and industrial automation (plant operation, fault diagnosis, causal and physical modelling), product design (function structures), and forecasting for cyber-physical systems
size: over 100 questions: over 80 on the two plants (45 for RQ1, 20 for RQ2, the rest for RQ4) and 20 on product design (pp. 3, 8, 10), plus 200 forecasting samples from two datasets (p7); four models: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct hosted locally, and GPT-4o (p5)
source_of_items: expert-written by the authors from a real glass-foaming plant, a simulated production plant and product-design function structures (pp. 3, 6-7, 11); some causal problems 'were created only for the present article' (p13); forecasting data from two existing datasets, Three-Tank and ETTh1 (p14)
has_gold_traces: no: the paper describes no reference solutions or worked traces; the rated answers and scores are published in the repository (p7)
evaluation: rubric: a holistic three-point rating (0, 0.5, 1) of the least accurate of several answers to each question, averaged per category (p5); MSE for forecasting (p7, Table 5 p16). No final-answer matching and no step-level scoring.
human_validation: The ratings are themselves human judgements, but the paper does not say who rated the answers, how many raters there were, or how far they agreed; no agreement statistic is reported (p5). No validation of the questions is described beyond their derivation from the two plants and the design models (pp. 3, 6-7).
contamination_measures: none stated; the questions are new, some written for this paper (pp. 3, 13), and the dataset is public (pp. 3, 18)

engtrace_use.sentence: Yet neither abstract logical deduction nor algorithmic proficiency transfers to reliable reasoning under physical constraints (Heesch et al., 2025). (S-M3, closing the mathematics-and-coding paragraph)
engtrace_use.explanation: The paper does not study transfer. It evaluates four LLMs only on its own engineering questions and measures neither mathematical nor coding proficiency, so it cannot show that either fails to transfer (pp. 3, 5). What it does find is narrower: physical modelling, which 'requires integration of numerical reasoning, causal dependencies, and physical constraints', proved difficult for all models (scores 0.13 to 0.50, p14), and the models struggle with 'abstract reasoning, formal modeling, and context-sensitive engineering logic' (p1). Its framing even runs against the May sentence's: abstraction is a weakness it reports in engineering itself (type-level concepts, pp. 8-9), not a strength that fails to transfer, and it finds models do better on symbolic tasks, with logical diagnosis, including Python code generation, 'easy for most of the evaluated LLMs' (pp. 13, 18). The sentence also omits what matters most for EngTrace: this is itself an engineering evaluation, which the engineering paragraph never discusses. It scores answers by a holistic rubric rather than by outcome matching (p5), against S-E3's claim, and it criticises evaluations built from 'simplified use cases, often adapted from examination materials where correctness is easily verifiable' (pp. 1-2), a critique EngTrace's textbook-style templates must answer.

suggested_wording: Heesch et al. (2025) pose over 100 questions drawn from a real glass-foaming plant, a simulated production line and product-design function structures to four LLMs, rate the worst of repeated answers on a three-point scale, and find that the models handle local, sequential reasoning but fail at type-level abstraction, multi-variable dependencies and formal and physical modelling.
facts_to_cite: Over 100 questions derived from production-oriented engineering scenarios: a real glass-foaming plant and a simulated discrete-manufacturing plant (over 80 questions) and 20 product-design questions on function structures, plus forecasting on 200 time-series samples (pp. 1, 3, 6-7).
Four LLMs were evaluated: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct hosted locally, and GPT-4o (p5).
Each question was posed several times and only the least accurate answer was scored, on a three-point scale whose middle and top points correspond to junior- and senior-engineer reasoning (p5).

Models did well on iterative consistency, state transitions and sequential understanding, and poorly on type-level concept generation, multi-variable dependency resolution, recognising design absurdities, strong-fault logical modelling and physical modelling (Tables 1-4, pp. 9-14).
Physical modelling, which needs numerical reasoning, causal dependencies and physical constraints together, scored 0.13 to 0.50 across the four models (p14, Table 4).
GPT-4o outperformed the locally hosted models on nearly every dimension except forecasting (p17); specialised LSTM and DLinear baselines beat all four LLMs at forecasting (pp. 15-16).

The authors argue that earlier engineering evaluations rely on 'simplified use cases, often adapted from examination materials where correctness is easily verifiable', or on ad hoc scenarios (pp. 1-2).
The dataset, rated answers and scores are public (pp. 3, 7).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: the engineering domain (production and industrial automation, fault diagnosis, product design; pp. 6-7, 11), touching EngTrace's industrial branch; graded credit for partial correctness (p5); concern with reliability across repeated answers (worst-of-repeats scoring, p5), which parallels EngTrace's decoding repeats. Lacks: generated instances (a static, hand-written set); gold traces or reference solutions (none described); step-level evaluation (a holistic rating of each answer); any validation of the rating (no rater identity or agreement statistic, p5); quantitative engineering calculation (the plant and design questions are mostly qualitative or symbolic, and forecasting is scored by MSE); and contamination measures beyond novelty (the set is public, p3).
notes: Placement: the May text uses this paper only in the mathematics-and-coding paragraph, yet it is direct prior work on evaluating LLMs for engineering and belongs in the engineering paragraph. Its holistic rubric contradicts S-E3's 'existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching'. Its critique of examination-style evaluations with easily verified answers (pp. 1-2) applies to EngTrace's design, and the revised text should answer it by naming the trade-off: EngTrace keeps verifiable problems so that every step can be checked against a gold trace, whereas Heesch et al. gain realism but rely on an unvalidated holistic rating. The transfer claim of S-M3 needs a different source, or should be dropped. The paper never names its dataset; the repository is imb-hsu/Wrenchmark (p7). The number of RQ4 questions is not given (over 80 for RQ1, RQ2 and RQ4 together, p3). Small oddity: Table 2's caption speaks of 'spatial structures' for the relations questions (p10).
